title: Reading an online assessment
objectives: Triage an assessment's problems and plan the minutes before writing code.

screens.title: Which problem pays best per minute
screens.prose: Reported assessments set two problems in 60 minutes, or three in 90. Platforms differ: some score each hidden test group, some only a fully passed problem. You ranked problems in `contests` l14-which-first. New here: partial credit and a minute budget.

lines: P1: 40 points in 20 minutes. The small groups alone: 12 points in 6.
P2: 60 points in 35 minutes. The small groups alone: 25 points in 12.
P3: 90 points in 50 minutes. The small groups alone: 30 points in 18.

screens.question: Which problem earns the most points per minute if you solve it in full?

options.text: P1
P2
options.why: You picked the middle problem. Its $60 / 35 \approx 1.71$ is the lowest rate of the three.

options.text: P3
options.why: You picked the biggest score. Its rate is $90 / 50 = 1.8$, and P1 earns 2.0.

options.text: They tie
options.why: You assumed the rates match. They are 2.0, 1.71 and 1.8.

hints.text: Divide each full score by its full minutes.
P1 is 40 points in 20 minutes.

feedback.correct: P1 pays 2.0 points a minute, ahead of P3 at 1.8 and P2 at 1.71.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Points divided by minutes gives the rate.

byKey.c: P3 has the most points, but $90 / 50 = 1.8$ is below 2.0.

explain.text: Divide each score by its minutes: 2.0, 1.71 and 1.8. The largest score, P3, is not the best price per minute.

screens.title: Take them by rate
screens.prose: Take whole problems in order of points per minute: P1, then P3, then P2. Skip any that no longer fits in the 62 minutes. Nothing partial yet.

screens.title: The best plan, in code
screens.prose: Listing every choice is $3^n$ plans, which fails on a long paper. Build a table over minutes instead, one problem at a time.

params.title: best_plan(problems, budget)
lines: Each problem is [full_points, full_minutes, partial_points, partial_minutes].
Choose full, partial or skip for every problem.
Return the most points earned in at most budget minutes.
best[m] is the most points that m minutes can earn.

screens.question: Write `best_plan(problems, budget)`.

tests.setup: import random; random.seed(1); ps = [(lambda fm, fp: [fp, fm, random.randint(1, fp), random.randint(2, fm)])(random.randint(5, 40), random.randint(10, 100)) for _ in range(60)]

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. They cover small papers, a zero budget, an empty paper and 60 problems with a budget of 600.

hints.text: What is best[m] before any problem is read?
Zero points for every m. A problem can only improve it.
For each problem, copy best. At each m, try full and partial from best[m - minutes]. Return best[budget].

feedback.correct: One table over minutes, updated once per problem.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: P3 in full and P2 in part fit in 55 minutes: 100 points.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: with no minutes nothing can be earned.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: at 14 minutes only a partial fits.
byKey.test-7: Test 7: the partial costs as much as the full, so take the full.
byKey.test-8: Test 8: the partial costs 5 minutes and fits in 10.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 has 60 problems. Trying every choice would take $3^{60}$ steps.

explain.text: For each problem we copy the table, then try full and partial from the row of earlier minutes. Each problem costs one pass over the minutes, so the work is problems times budget. Choosing from the old copy stops one problem being used twice.

screens.title: Test groups
screens.prose: A statement lists three groups: $n \le 1{,}000$, $n \le 100{,}000$ and $n \le 1{,}000{,}000$. Count about $10^8$ steps a second, as in `contests` l2. Mark each group a solution passes.

params.title: Hidden test groups
lines: Group 1: n up to 1,000.
Group 2: n up to 100,000.
Group 3: n up to 1,000,000.

screens.question: Fill in Yes or No for each solution and group.

hints.text: Count steps at the top of each group.
A quadratic solution takes $n^2$ steps: $10^6$, then $10^{10}$, then $10^{12}$.
Only $10^6$ is under $10^8$. An $n \log n$ solution takes about $2 \times 10^7$ steps at the top group.

feedback.correct: The quadratic solution earns the first group only. The other two earn all three.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the step count with $10^8$.

explain.text: Squaring $10^3$ gives $10^6$ steps, which is fine. Squaring $10^5$ gives $10^{10}$, which is not. The quadratic solution scores the small group and stops there.

lines.text: Read every statement to the end
Note each limit and the points of each group
Estimate the full and partial minutes of each problem
Rank by points per minute and settle the partials
Set a time box for each problem

hints.text: What must you know before you can rank anything?
You need every statement read, with limits and points noted.
Read, note, estimate, rank, box, then start. Code comes last.

feedback.correct: Read and note first, then estimate, rank and box, and start last.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ranking needs the estimates, and estimates need the reading.

byKey.a6: Starting is the last step. Until you have ranked the problems you do not know which is surest.
byKey.a4: Ranking needs the estimates of step 3 first.

explain.text: You cannot rank problems you have not read, and you cannot rank them without minute estimates. Boxes come after the ranking, and code after the boxes.

lines.text: Copy `best` into `new`, which also covers skipping

hints.text: What does skipping a problem do to the table?
It leaves every entry as it was, so start from a copy.
Copy first, try both prices, keep the larger, then swap the table in.

feedback.correct: Copy, try full and partial, keep the larger, then swap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Skipping is the copy, so it comes first.

byKey.s5: You swapped too early. The table must be finished before `best` is replaced.

explain.text: The copy is the skip option. Each price looks back in the old table, so a problem is used at most once. After the pass, the new table replaces the old.

screens.question: Which plan earns the most?

B in full and A in part: 57 minutes, 80 points
options.why: You added 45 and 12 to get 57. That is over the 55 minutes left.

options.text: Both in full: 85 minutes, 110 points
options.why: You ignored the budget. Both in full need 85 minutes.

options.text: Both in part: 27 minutes, 45 points
options.why: You left 28 minutes unused. Swapping A's partial for A's full fits in 55.

hints.text: List the plans that fit in 55 minutes.
A in full takes 40 and leaves 15.
15 minutes is exactly B's partial. B in full plus A in part needs 57, which is too many.

feedback.correct: A in full and B in part fill the 55 minutes and earn 75. Nothing else fits for more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the minutes of each plan to the 55 left.

explain.text: A in full with B in part fills the 55 minutes and earns 75, the most that fits. To rehearse, sit the mock at `#exam/mock-oa-code`: two Python problems in 60 minutes. It scores a problem only when every hidden test passes.

ideas: Read every problem first. Note the limits and the points, and estimate full and partial minutes for each.
Choose full, partial or skip for each problem so the points are most for the minutes you have.
Check the scoring rule first: it decides whether a partial is worth submitting. Where groups score, count steps at each group's top $n$.

formula.name: Rate of a problem
formula.note: Rank by rate, then check that a partial does not fill a gap better.

summary.trap: Allowing no partial credit, which leaves minutes unspent.

quiz.question: Problem X earns 36 points in 24 minutes. Problem Y earns 28 points in 14 minutes. Which has the higher rate?

options.text: Y, at 2.0 points a minute
X, because it earns more points
options.why: You compared the scores. Divide by the minutes: X gives 1.5 and Y gives 2.0.

options.text: They are equal
X, because it takes longer
options.why: A longer problem is not a better one. The rate is points over minutes.

feedback.correct: Y earns $28 / 14 = 2.0$ points a minute, X earns $36 / 24 = 1.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each score by its minutes.

byKey.b: You compared the scores, not the rates.

explain.text: A rate is points divided by minutes. X gives 1.5 and Y gives 2.0, so Y pays better per minute.

quiz.question: An assessment lasts 80 minutes. You read for 5 and keep 5 for a final check. How many minutes can you spend on solving?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take both the reading and the check from 80.

byKey.read: You took off only the reading. The final check also needs 5 minutes.
byKey.full: You used the whole length. Reading and checking come out of it.

explain.text: The budget is the length minus the reading and the final check. That leaves 70 minutes to spend across the problems.

quiz.question: A statement has two groups: $n \le 2{,}000$ and $n \le 300{,}000$. Your solution takes about $n^2$ steps. Which groups can it pass?

options.text: Only the first: $2{,}000^2 = 4 \times 10^6$ steps
Both: it is correct, so it passes every single group
options.why: You checked correctness but not speed. $300{,}000^2$ is $9 \times 10^{10}$ steps.

options.text: Neither: a quadratic solution is always too slow
options.why: You ruled out every quadratic solution. $4 \times 10^6$ steps is quick.

options.text: Only the second: larger groups are easier
options.why: Larger groups are harder. They have more steps.

feedback.correct: The first group needs $4 \times 10^6$ steps, the second $9 \times 10^{10}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the largest $n$ in each group.

byKey.b: A correct but slow solution fails the large group by time.
byKey.d: More input means more steps, not fewer.

explain.text: A slow solution still scores the small group. At $10^8$ steps a second, $4 \times 10^6$ is fast and $9 \times 10^{10}$ is not.

quiz.question: A problem pays 30 points for 25 minutes in full, or 12 points for 5 minutes in part. You have 8 minutes left. What do you take?

options.text: The partial: 12 points in 5 minutes
The full marks: 30 points is worth more
options.why: You compared points and ignored the minutes. Full marks needs 25, and you have 8.

options.text: Neither: a partial is not worth submitting
options.why: You ruled out partial credit. It earns 12 points now.

options.text: Start the full marks and hope to finish
options.why: You hoped to finish in 8 minutes what needs 25. Take the sure points.

feedback.correct: Only the partial fits in 8 minutes, and it earns 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each price with the 8 minutes left.

byKey.b: Full marks needs 25 minutes. You have 8.
byKey.d: A guess at 25 minutes of work in 8 earns nothing.

explain.text: Full marks needs 25 minutes and only 8 remain. The partial costs 5 and earns 12, so it is the only plan that scores.
